transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I guess what brings me in is I just can’t seem to get past how I look anymore, especially my face and my hands. I know that probably sounds a little foolish at my age, and I’ve worked outdoors most of my life, so maybe some of it is expected, but it feels like every crack, every spot, every bit of sagging or roughness is just… right there for everybody to see.

When I have to go into town, like to deal with a banker or someone at the county office, I get this feeling they’re looking at my face or staring at my hands, like they’re noticing how worn out I look. My wife tells me I just look like a man who’s worked outside, nothing strange, but I can’t really take that in. To me it looks rough, old, weather-beaten in a bad way, and I keep getting stuck on it. That’s the main thing, I suppose.
Are you worried about anything else besides how you look?

I don’t know… not in the same way, I don’t think. I mean, there are the usual worries a person has—money, keeping things running, getting older, whether I’m keeping up the way I should—but when you ask what really gets stuck in my head, it’s mostly this thing about my appearance.

I’m trying to think if there’s some other big fear or concern I’m missing, but nothing comes to mind like that. It all seems to circle back to how I look when people see me, especially up close. If I’m worried about going somewhere, it’s usually because I’m thinking about what they’ll notice on me, not some separate thing. So… no, not really anything else that stands out.
Has your concern about how you look stopped you from doing things you would normally do or from seeing people you know?

Yes… yeah, it has. More than I like to admit, honestly.

There’ve been times I was supposed to talk with bankers or sit down with people about decisions for the farm, and I just kept putting it off because I couldn’t get myself to look… acceptable, I guess. I’d wash up, change shirts, look at my face and hands, and then I’d start thinking, “I can’t sit across from someone looking like this.” So I’d miss the call or delay it, tell myself I’d handle it tomorrow or next week, but really it was because I couldn’t stand the idea of them seeing me close up.

And with the retreat and craft sales, people have wanted photos for promotion, just normal pictures to show what we do, and I’ve pretty much stopped agreeing to be in them. I’ll offer to take the picture or say someone else should be in it, anything to avoid being seen that way. It’s embarrassing, because it does get in the way of things I’d normally just do.
Is it always your face and hands that you're concerned about, or are there other parts of your body that bother you as well?

It’s mainly my face and my hands, yes. Those are the things I keep coming back to. I mean, I can notice other things about getting older, sure, but it doesn’t grab hold of me the same way.

My face is what I worry people are looking at when I’m sitting across from them, especially someone like a banker or someone at a county office, where the lighting’s bright and you’re close enough for them to see every spot and line and bit of sagging. And my hands… they’re right out there too, signing papers or shaking hands or just resting on a table, and all I can think is how cracked and rough and worn they look.

My wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, and maybe that’s all it is, but it doesn’t feel that way to me. It feels like it’s too noticeable, like those are the first things people see. So, no, I wouldn’t say it moves around much. It’s mostly my face and hands.
How much distress would you say these concerns about your face and hands cause you on a daily basis?

On a daily basis… it’s a lot. I don’t know how to put a number on it, but it wears on me pretty steadily.

It’s not just a quick thought like, “Oh, I look tired today.” It’s more like I catch sight of my face or my hands and then I can’t quite get past it. I start seeing every rough patch, every crack, the spots, the sagging around my face, and then I imagine that’s exactly what other people are seeing too. Especially if I know I have to deal with a banker or someone at the county office, or anybody where I’m sitting close across from them. I’ll be thinking about the lighting, where my hands are, whether they’re looking at my skin instead of listening to me.

My wife tells me I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, and I know she means to reassure me. And maybe that’s what other people would say too. But it doesn’t feel like that inside my own head. It feels like I look… worn out, rough, kind of exposed. Like it’s all right there for people to judge.

So, yeah, it causes me distress most days. Some days I can push through it better than others, but it’s there in the background a lot.
Are your concerns about your appearance focused on any specific features or flaws that you think are particularly noticeable or unattractive?

Yes. It’s pretty specific, I think. It’s my face and my hands, and not just in a general “I’m getting older” way. It’s the roughness, the cracks in my hands, the spots on my skin, and the way my face looks saggy and worn down. I get stuck on those things.

Like if I know I’m going to sit with a banker or someone from the county office, I start imagining them noticing all of it right away. The lines, the weathered look, the skin on my hands when I sign something or put them on the table. I’ll be talking, but in my head I’m thinking, “They’re looking at how bad my hands are,” or “My face looks awful in this light.”

My wife tells me I just look like someone who’s worked outdoors his whole life, and I suppose that should make sense. I mean, I have worked outdoors. But to me it doesn’t feel normal or respectable-looking. It feels like I look rough, worn out, unattractive… like those things are the first things people see when they look at me.
Have you avoided any important life events or activities because of your concerns about how you look?

Yes… I have. I don’t like saying that, because it sounds foolish when I hear it out loud, but yes.

It’s gotten in the way of things I really should’ve handled. I’ve missed calls with bankers, or I’ve let them go and then not called back right away, because I knew the next step would be sitting down with them in person, across a desk, under those bright office lights. And I’d start thinking, well, I need to get myself looking halfway decent first — my face not looking so rough, my hands not cracked up and ugly — and then I just… wouldn’t do it. Then a farm decision that needed making would sit there longer than it should have.

And with the retreat and the craft sales, there are times they’ve wanted pictures for promotion, just simple things, nothing fancy. Me standing there, or holding something, or being part of the farm image, I guess. I’ve stopped agreeing to those. I’ll make an excuse, or I’ll say someone else would look better in it, but really it’s because I don’t want my face or hands in the photo. Once it’s taken, then people can look at it as long as they want, and that bothers me.

So, yes, I’ve avoided things. Not every single thing, but enough that it’s caused problems.
Do you think other people actually notice these flaws in your face and hands, or is it more that you're worried they might?

I guess it’s both, but if I’m being honest, in the moment it feels like they actually notice. It doesn’t feel like just a vague worry.

Like with my face and hands, I’ll be sitting across from a banker or someone at the county office, and I’m convinced they’re seeing the cracks in my hands, the spots, the rough skin, the sagging in my face. I’ll notice their eyes move even a little bit and my mind goes right to, “They saw it.” Maybe they’re just looking at a paper or glancing around like anyone would, but I read it as them noticing how worn I look.

My wife tells me I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, and I understand what she’s saying. I know that’s probably how some people would see it. But inside my head, it feels much worse than that. It feels like I look rough and old and kind of… exposed, like those things are obvious and hard to look away from.

So yes, part of me knows I may be worrying they’re noticing more than they really are. But when I’m actually there, face-to-face with someone, it feels like they’re staring right at those flaws.
Do you think your appearance is actually as bad as you imagine it to be, or is it worse in your mind than in reality?

I think… I think part of me knows it’s worse in my mind than it probably is in real life. I can say that sitting here, anyway. My wife tells me I look like a man who’s worked outdoors, and that’s true — I have. I’ve been outside most of my life, using my hands, getting sun and wind and all of that. So, rationally, I can understand that maybe the cracks and spots and sagging don’t look as terrible to other people as they do to me.

But that’s not how it feels when I’m looking at myself, or when I’m sitting across from someone. Then it feels like it’s exactly as bad as I imagine. Like my face looks rough and worn down, and my hands look cracked and old, and that’s what they’re seeing before anything else. Especially with bankers or county people — someone across a desk, close enough to see everything. I’ll be thinking the whole time that they’re noticing the spots, the sagging, the rough skin, even if they don’t say anything.

So… I guess the honest answer is, I know there’s a chance I’m making it bigger in my head. But it doesn’t feel like just imagination. It feels real to me when I’m in it.
Do you think there's one particular flaw or feature in your face or hands that bothers you the most?

It’s hard to pick just one, because it sort of all runs together in my mind. But if I had to say, it’s probably the roughness — the cracked-up, worn look of my hands and the way my face looks saggy and weathered.

My hands bother me a lot because they’re right there in front of people. If I’m sitting with a banker or someone from the county, I’m handing over papers, signing things, resting my hands on the desk, and I feel like the cracks and spots are just… obvious. Like they make me look dirty or old, even if I know that’s not fair. I’ve worked outdoors for years, so of course my hands aren’t going to look smooth, but I can’t seem to see them that way.

And my face too — the sagging, the rough skin, the spots. That gets to me because I can’t hide it. My wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outside, and maybe that’s true, but I don’t feel that way when someone’s looking at me. I feel like they’re seeing how worn down I look before they hear a word I’m saying.

So I don’t know if it’s one particular spot, exactly. It’s more this whole rough, aged, worn-out look in my face and hands that I can’t get past.
Do you think you would still feel anxious or self-conscious in social situations if you felt completely satisfied with your appearance?

Honestly, I think if I felt completely satisfied with how I looked, I’d probably be a lot less anxious in those situations. Maybe not perfectly comfortable — I don’t know — but the thing that really gets in my head is my appearance.

What brings me in is that I can’t get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. It’s like once I’m sitting across from a banker, or someone at the county office, I’m not just thinking about whatever business I’m there for. I’m thinking, “They’re looking at my hands. They see the cracks. They see the spots. They see how saggy my face looks.” And then I start feeling exposed, like I’m sitting there under a bright light or something.

If I didn’t have that running through my mind, I think I could probably just talk to people more normally. My wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, and maybe if I could really believe that — not just hear it, but feel satisfied with it — then I don’t think I’d be nearly as self-conscious. It’s not that every social situation is the problem by itself. It’s that I’m carrying this feeling that my face and hands look worn out and obvious, and that everyone close enough to me is noticing.
Do you think people are judging you as a person based on how you look, or is it more that you're worried about them noticing specific flaws in your appearance?

I think it’s more the second one… more that I’m worried they’re noticing the specific things. The cracks in my hands, the spots, the sagging in my face, that rough sort of worn-out look. I don’t know that I sit there thinking, “They think I’m a bad person,” exactly. It’s not quite that.

It’s more like I feel exposed, like those features are the first thing they see. If I’m across from a banker or someone at the county office, I’ll be trying to listen, but my mind keeps going to my hands on the desk or my face under the lights. I imagine them staring at the rough skin, the cracks, the age spots, the sagging. And even if they’re just being normal, I read into it.

My wife tells me I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, and I know there’s truth in that. I mean, I have worked outdoors most of my life. But what brings me in is that I can’t get past the feeling that it looks worse than that — like it looks neglected or ugly or too old. So it’s less that I think they’re judging my whole character, and more that I’m sure they’re noticing those flaws and that I can’t stop thinking about it.
Do you think that others actually see you as you perceive yourself, or is it just your own self-image that is distorted?

I go back and forth on that. Part of me knows my wife is probably seeing me more fairly than I see myself. She says I just look like a man who’s worked outside for a long time, and I know that makes sense. I’ve had sun, dirt, weather, tools in my hands for years, so of course my skin isn’t going to look like somebody who sat in an office.

But when I’m actually with other people, especially someone like a banker or somebody at the county office, it doesn’t feel like it’s just in my head. It feels like they’re staring right at the cracks in my hands, the spots, the sagging in my face — like all that rough, worn look is the main thing they notice. I’ll be sitting there trying to listen, and I’m thinking about where my hands are, whether they’re looking at them, whether the light is making my face look worse.

So… I guess if I’m being honest, there must be some distortion in how I see myself, because other people don’t react the way I think they will. My wife doesn’t see it the way I do. But it feels very real to me in the moment. What brings me in is that I can’t get past it — this feeling that my face and hands look rough and old and obvious, even when someone else might just see a man who’s worked outdoors.
Do you think you would be satisfied with your appearance if you could change just one thing about your face or hands?

I don’t know if just one thing would do it, honestly. That’s part of what’s frustrating. If you told me, “Okay, we can fix the cracks in your hands,” I think I’d feel better for a while, because those really bother me. I notice them when I’m sitting at a desk with someone, like at the bank or the county office, and I’ll try to tuck my hands away or keep them still so they don’t draw attention.

But then I think my mind would probably go right to the spots, or the sagging in my face, or just that whole rough, worn-out look. It’s not one little mark, exactly. It’s the way my face and hands together make me feel like I look older, rougher, more beat-up than I should. My wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, and I know she means that kindly — and maybe she’s right — but I can’t seem to feel that way when I’m around other people.

So if I could change one thing, maybe I’d pick my hands, because they’re right there in front of people. But I’m not sure I’d be satisfied overall. I think I’d still be looking for what else looks bad. That’s what brings me in, really — I can’t get past the feeling that they’re staring at the cracks, the spots, the sagging, all of it.
Do you think your concerns about your appearance would decrease if you were in a situation where you felt completely accepted and liked by the people around you?

Maybe a little, but I don’t think it would go away. If I really felt accepted, like I knew the people around me weren’t looking down on me, I suppose I’d be less tense for a while. With my wife, for example, she tells me I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, and I know she’s not trying to hurt me. I believe her in a way.

But even then, I still get stuck on it. What brings me in is that I can’t get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. It’s like once I’m in front of someone — especially a banker or someone at the county office — my mind goes right to the cracks in my hands, the spots, the sagging in my face. Even if they’re being perfectly polite, even if they probably don’t care, I feel like that’s what they’re seeing.

So if I felt completely liked, I think it might take some of the sting out of it. But I don’t know that it would stop the thoughts. I’d still be aware of my hands on the desk, or how the light is hitting my face, or whether I look worn-out and older than I should. It’s not just whether they accept me, I guess. It’s that I can’t stop seeing those things myself, and then I assume everybody else sees them too.
Do you think your concerns about your appearance would improve if you were able to hide or cover up the specific flaws that bother you?

Maybe some, yes. I mean, if I could cover my hands better, or if there was some way my face didn’t show all that weathered look so much, I think I’d feel less exposed. When I’m sitting across from somebody at the bank or the county office, my hands feel like they’re just right there under a spotlight — the cracks, the rough skin, the spots. I’ll catch myself pulling them back or folding them under the table, like if they can’t see them then maybe I can pay attention to what they’re saying.

But I don’t think covering it would really fix what’s going on in my head. Because what brings me in is that I can’t get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. Even if I hid one part, I’d still be wondering if they noticed the sagging in my face, or whether the light was making me look older and more beat-up. My wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, and I try to take that in, but when I’m around those kinds of people, it feels like every one of them is staring right at the cracks and spots and all of it.

So hiding it might help me get through a moment, maybe make me less nervous sitting there. But I think I’d still know it was there, and I’d still be thinking about it. That’s the hard part — it follows me even when nobody says anything.
Do you think your concerns about your appearance are because of something specifically wrong with how you look, or is it more that you just don't like how you look in general?

I think it’s both, but more… specific things, I guess. It’s not like I wake up and just say, “I hate everything about myself.” It’s more that I can’t get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. The cracks in my hands, the spots, the sagging in my face — those are the things my eyes go right to, and then I feel like that’s all anyone else can see too.

Especially with people like bankers or someone at the county office. I’ll be sitting there trying to talk business, and instead of listening properly I’m thinking, “They’re looking at my hands. They’re seeing how cracked and old they look.” Or if the light is on my face, I’m thinking they can see how worn-out I look. My wife tells me I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, and I know that’s probably true in a plain sense, but it doesn’t settle it for me.

So I wouldn’t say it’s just a general dislike. It’s more that certain parts feel wrong to me, and then those parts make my whole appearance feel rough and beat-up. I get stuck on them.
Do you think your appearance is ever not noticeable to others, or do you always assume people are looking at the flaws you see in yourself?

I wish I could say I know there are times it isn’t noticeable, and maybe, logically, that has to be true. I mean, people have their own lives, they’re busy, they’re thinking about paperwork or money or whatever the meeting is about. My wife says that to me too — she says I’m just a man who’s worked outdoors, and that most people probably don’t think twice about it.

But in the moment, no, I usually assume they’re seeing it. Especially people like bankers or county office people, people who look neat and clean and like they spend their days indoors. I’ll be sitting across from them and I can feel my hands there on the desk, and I’m thinking about the cracks, the rough skin, the spots. Then I start thinking about my face too, like how worn it looks, the sagging, the weathered look. It feels like those are the first things they notice, even if they don’t say anything.

So I guess I can understand that maybe my appearance isn’t always noticeable to others, but I don’t really feel that way when I’m around people. What brings me in is I can’t get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. Once I notice it, I just assume everybody else can see exactly what I’m seeing.
Do you think your concerns about your appearance are focused on specific flaws or is it a general feeling of not liking how you look?

It’s more specific flaws, I think. I mean, I don’t sit there thinking every single part of me is wrong, exactly. What brings me in is that I just can’t get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. My hands especially — the cracks, the spots, the rough skin — and then my face, the sagging and that weathered look. Once I notice those things, it kind of spreads, like then I feel like my whole appearance looks old and beat-up.

And it’s worse around certain people, like bankers or people at the county office. They look polished, clean, like they haven’t spent their lives outside working, and I’ll be sitting there thinking they’re staring right at my hands or my face. Even if they’re just looking at paperwork, in my mind it feels like they’ve already noticed the cracks and the spots and all that.

My wife tells me I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, and I know she means that kindly, and maybe that’s how other people see it too. But I don’t feel that way when I’m in it. It’s not just a general “I don’t like myself.” It’s those particular things — my face and hands looking so rough and worn — that I get stuck on.
Do you think you would feel better about your appearance if you could change one specific thing about your face or hands?

I think I tell myself I would, yes. Like if my hands weren’t so cracked and spotted, or if my face didn’t look so saggy and weathered, I imagine I’d be able to sit across from someone and not have that running in my head the whole time.

But then I don’t know if it would really stop, because it’s not just one tiny thing, you know? It’s the whole worn look of my face and hands together. When I’m with a banker or someone at the county office, I’ll notice my hands on the desk, and then I’m thinking about the cracks, then the spots, then whether my face looks just as rough under the lights. It builds on itself.

My wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, and maybe if I could believe that, that would help more than changing one thing. But if you asked me what I’d change, it would be the roughness — the cracks and spots on my hands, and that sagging, beat-up look in my face. I feel like if those were better, I wouldn’t feel so exposed all the time.
